chapter_text:
CHAPTER 6 - ROOT SYSTEM

Introduction

The plant body of a flowering plant is divided into two main systems: the underground ROOT SYSTEM and the aerial SHOOT SYSTEM. The root is normally the underground, non-green, descending part of the plant that develops from the RADICLE of the germinating seed. Unlike the shoot, the root does not bear leaves, buds or flowers, it grows towards gravity (positively geotropic) and away from light (negatively phototropic), and it is attracted towards water (positively hydrotropic). All the roots of a single plant taken together form its ROOT SYSTEM. This chapter studies the kinds of root systems, the external regions along a young root, the internal (anatomical) structure of dicot and monocot roots, the many ways in which roots are modified for special jobs, and finally the functions that roots perform for the plant.

6.1 TYPES OF ROOT SYSTEMS

When a seed germinates, the radicle grows out and forms the PRIMARY ROOT. What happens next decides the type of root system.

TAP ROOT SYSTEM. In most dicotyledonous plants the primary root continues to grow, becoming a thick, long main root called the TAP ROOT. From it arise smaller LATERAL (secondary and tertiary) roots in acropetal order (older ones near the base, younger ones near the tip). The tap root grows vertically downwards and penetrates deep into the soil. Because it develops from the radicle, the tap root system is the true, normal root system. Examples: mustard, gram, mango, neem, carrot and radish. The deep tap root anchors the plant firmly and can draw water from deep layers of the soil.

FIBROUS ROOT SYSTEM. In most monocotyledonous plants (such as grasses, wheat, maize, rice and onion) the primary root is short-lived. It soon dies and is replaced by a cluster of thin, thread-like roots of more or less equal size that arise from the base of the stem. This bunch of slender roots is the FIBROUS ROOT SYSTEM. Fibrous roots do not go very deep; they spread out just below the surface and bind the top soil well, which makes grasses good for checking soil erosion.

ADVENTITIOUS ROOT SYSTEM. Roots that arise from any part of the plant OTHER than the radicle - from the stem, nodes, leaves or branches - are called ADVENTITIOUS ROOTS. The prop roots of banyan, the stilt roots of maize and sugarcane, and the roots that grow from a cutting of rose or sugarcane are adventitious. Fibrous roots of monocots are themselves adventitious in origin because they too do not come from the radicle. Adventitious roots may perform normal functions or special ones such as extra support, storage or climbing.

6.2 REGIONS OF A ROOT

If we examine a young root from its tip upwards, we can recognise four distinct regions.

ROOT CAP. The very tip of the root is covered by a thimble-like cap of loosely arranged parenchyma cells called the ROOT CAP. It protects the delicate growing tip as the root is pushed through the hard, abrasive soil. The outer cells of the cap are constantly worn away and are replaced from within, and the cap cells secrete a slimy mucilage that lubricates the passage of the root. Some water plants have a root pocket instead of a true root cap.

REGION OF MERISTEMATIC ACTIVITY (region of cell division). Just behind the root cap lies a small region a few millimetres long whose cells are small, thin-walled, densely packed and rich in cytoplasm with prominent nuclei. These meristematic cells divide again and again by mitosis and are responsible for the growth in length of the root. This region has no root hairs.

REGION OF ELONGATION. Above the meristematic region the newly formed cells stop dividing and instead ENLARGE and elongate rapidly, absorbing water and increasing greatly in length. This elongation of cells pushes the root tip deeper into the soil. The cells here also begin to differentiate.

REGION OF MATURATION (region of root hairs). Still higher up the cells reach their full size and mature into permanent tissues - epidermis, cortex, vascular tissue and so on. From the epidermal cells of this region grow numerous fine, delicate, unicellular outgrowths called ROOT HAIRS. Each root hair is a tubular extension of a single epidermal cell. Root hairs enormously increase the surface area of the root and are the chief site of ABSORPTION of water and dissolved mineral salts from the soil. Above the root-hair zone the older part of the root becomes the region of permanent tissue that may bear lateral roots.

6.3 INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A DICOT ROOT

A transverse section (T.S.) of a young dicot root, seen under the microscope, shows the following tissues arranged from the outside inwards.

EPIDERMIS (EPIBLEMA). The outermost single layer of thin-walled cells, also called the epiblema or rhizodermis. It has no cuticle and no stomata; instead many of its cells extend outward as root hairs. It protects the inner tissues and absorbs water.

CORTEX. Beneath the epidermis lies a broad zone of several layers of thin-walled, rounded PARENCHYMA cells with conspicuous intercellular spaces. The cortex stores food and helps conduct water from the root hairs towards the inner vascular tissue.

ENDODERMIS. The innermost layer of the cortex is a single, compact ring of barrel-shaped cells called the ENDODERMIS. Its radial and transverse walls carry a band-like thickening of a waterproof, corky material (suberin) known as the CASPARIAN STRIP. The Casparian strips block the movement of water through the cell walls and force all incoming water and minerals to pass through the living cytoplasm of the endodermal cells, so the endodermis acts as a check-post that controls what enters the vascular cylinder.

PERICYCLE. Just inside the endodermis is a layer (one or a few cells thick) of thin-walled cells called the PERICYCLE. It gives rise to LATERAL ROOTS and, in dicots, takes part in secondary growth (it produces part of the vascular cambium and the cork cambium).

VASCULAR BUNDLES (radial arrangement). In the centre the xylem and phloem occur as separate bundles arranged on different radii, in a RADIAL manner. The xylem is EXARCH (the oldest, first-formed protoxylem lies towards the outside and the metaxylem towards the centre). A dicot root usually has a SMALL number of xylem and phloem strands - typically two to six (di-, tri-, tetra- or hexarch); commonly it is tetrarch.

PITH. In a typical dicot root the pith at the centre is very small or almost absent, because the xylem strands extend nearly to the centre.

6.4 INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF A MONOCOT ROOT

A T.S. of a monocot root is broadly similar to that of a dicot root - it too shows epidermis, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, a radial and exarch arrangement of vascular tissue, and a central pith. The important POINTS OF DIFFERENCE are:

- POLYARCH vascular bundles. The monocot root has MANY (usually more than six, often very many) xylem and phloem strands arranged in a ring - it is polyarch, whereas the dicot root has only a few strands.

- LARGE PITH. The pith at the centre of a monocot root is LARGE and well developed, because the numerous xylem bundles do not reach the centre.

- NO SECONDARY GROWTH. Monocot roots do not have a cambium and so show no secondary growth; they remain the same thickness throughout life. The pericycle here produces only lateral roots and not vascular cambium.

Apart from these, the epidermis, cortex and endodermis are essentially the same in both, and in both the xylem is exarch and the bundles are radial. These anatomical features are commonly used to tell a dicot root from a monocot root under the microscope.

6.5 MODIFICATIONS OF ROOTS

Roots are often modified in form and structure to perform special functions in addition to, or instead of, their normal jobs.

STORAGE (FLESHY) ROOTS. Roots may swell up by storing large amounts of food, mainly starch and sugars. In the TAP ROOT storage type the main tap root becomes fleshy: it is conical in carrot, fusiform (spindle-shaped, swollen in the middle and tapering at both ends) in radish, and napiform (top-shaped, swollen and rounded) in turnip and beet. In some plants the ADVENTITIOUS roots store food, as in the tuberous roots of sweet potato and the fascicled (clustered) roots of dahlia and Asparagus.

RESPIRATORY ROOTS (PNEUMATOPHORES). Plants growing in marshy, waterlogged or saline soil, such as the mangroves (for example Rhizophora and Avicennia in tidal swamps), suffer from a lack of oxygen around their roots. Some of their roots grow VERTICALLY UPWARDS out of the mud into the air. These negatively geotropic roots are called PNEUMATOPHORES; they bear small pores (lenticels or pneumathodes) through which air reaches the underground roots for respiration.

SUPPORTING (MECHANICAL) ROOTS. Several adventitious roots give extra mechanical support. PROP ROOTS (pillar roots) hang down from the horizontal branches of the banyan tree, reach the soil, thicken and grow into pillar-like supports that hold up the huge spreading crown. STILT ROOTS arise from the lower nodes of the stem and grow obliquely downwards into the soil to brace the plant, as in maize, sugarcane and screw-pine (Pandanus). CLIMBING ROOTS arise from the nodes of weak-stemmed climbers such as money plant (Pothos) and betel, and cling to a support.

OTHER MODIFICATIONS. In parasitic plants such as Cuscuta (dodder) special sucking roots called HAUSTORIA penetrate the host stem and absorb food and water from it. In leguminous plants (gram, pea, bean) the roots bear small swellings called ROOT NODULES that house nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria; these bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use, enriching the soil. Some epiphytic orchids have hanging AERIAL ROOTS with a spongy tissue called velamen that absorbs moisture from the air.

6.6 FUNCTIONS OF ROOTS

The root performs several vital functions for the plant.

- ANCHORAGE (FIXATION). The most obvious function is to fix the plant firmly in the soil and hold the shoot upright against wind and its own weight. Deep tap roots and spreading fibrous roots both give a firm grip.

- ABSORPTION. Roots, chiefly through their root hairs, absorb water and dissolved mineral salts from the soil. The huge surface area provided by countless root hairs makes this absorption efficient.

- CONDUCTION. The absorbed water and minerals are conducted through the xylem of the root up into the stem and leaves, while food made in the leaves can be brought down and stored in the root.

- STORAGE. Roots, especially fleshy modified roots, store reserve food (starch and sugars) that the plant draws upon later, for example during regrowth or flowering.

- OTHER FUNCTIONS. Roots also help to hold the soil together and check soil erosion; some carry out special jobs such as respiration (pneumatophores), extra support (prop and stilt roots), nitrogen fixation (root nodules), and even vegetative reproduction (new plants arising from root cuttings, as in sweet potato and Dalbergia).

SUMMARY

- The root is the underground, non-green, positively geotropic part of the plant that develops from the radicle and lacks leaves and buds; all the roots together form the root system.
- Three types of root systems: tap root (from the radicle, deep, main root with laterals, typical of dicots), fibrous (a cluster of thin equal roots from the stem base, typical of monocots) and adventitious (arising from any part other than the radicle).
- A young root has four regions from the tip upwards: the protective root cap, the region of meristematic activity (cell division), the region of elongation, and the region of maturation that bears the absorbing root hairs.
- A dicot root in T.S. shows epidermis (epiblema) with root hairs, a broad parenchymatous cortex, an endodermis with Casparian strips, a pericycle that forms lateral roots, radial and exarch vascular bundles (a few strands, di- to hexarch, usually tetrarch) and little or no pith.
- A monocot root is similar but has many (polyarch) vascular strands, a large well-developed pith, and no secondary growth.
- Roots are modified for storage (conical carrot, fusiform radish, napiform turnip, tuberous sweet potato), respiration (pneumatophores of mangroves), support (prop roots of banyan, stilt roots of maize and sugarcane), and other jobs (haustoria of parasites, nitrogen-fixing root nodules, velamen of orchids).
- The main functions of roots are anchorage, absorption of water and minerals, conduction, and storage of food, along with soil binding and special functions.

topics.name: Types of Root Systems
topics.description: The three kinds of root systems: the tap root system (developing from the radicle, a deep main root with laterals, typical of dicots), the fibrous root system (a cluster of thin equal roots from the stem base, typical of monocots) and the adventitious root system (roots arising from any part of the plant other than the radicle).

topics.name: Regions of a Root
topics.description: The four external regions seen along a young root from the tip upwards: the protective root cap, the region of meristematic activity (cell division), the region of elongation, and the region of maturation that bears the water-absorbing root hairs.

topics.name: Internal Structure of a Dicot Root
topics.description: The transverse-section anatomy of a dicot root: epidermis (epiblema) with root hairs, parenchymatous cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle forming lateral roots, radial and exarch vascular bundles (a few strands, usually tetrarch) and little or no pith.

topics.name: Internal Structure of a Monocot Root
topics.description: The transverse-section anatomy of a monocot root and how it differs from a dicot root: many (polyarch) vascular strands, a large well-developed pith and absence of secondary growth, while sharing the epidermis, cortex, endodermis and radial exarch arrangement.

topics.name: Modifications of Roots
topics.description: Roots modified for special functions: storage (conical carrot, fusiform radish, napiform turnip, tuberous sweet potato), respiration (pneumatophores of mangroves), support (prop roots of banyan, stilt roots of maize and sugarcane) and others (parasitic haustoria, nitrogen-fixing root nodules, velamen roots of orchids).

topics.name: Functions of Roots
topics.description: The vital functions performed by roots: anchorage of the plant in the soil, absorption of water and mineral salts through root hairs, conduction of absorbed materials, storage of reserve food, and special roles such as soil binding, respiration, support and nitrogen fixation.

learning_outcomes.description: Define a root and a root system and identify the tap, fibrous and adventitious root systems with suitable examples of each.
Distinguish tap root, fibrous and adventitious root systems by their origin and form, and relate them to dicot and monocot plants.
Describe the four regions of a young root - root cap, region of meristematic activity, region of elongation and region of maturation with root hairs - and explain the role of each.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Internal Structure of a Dicot Root
learning_outcomes.description: Describe the internal transverse-section structure of a dicot root including epidermis, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, radial exarch vascular bundles and pith.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: Internal Structure of a Monocot Root
learning_outcomes.description: Describe the internal structure of a monocot root and compare it with a dicot root, noting polyarch vascular bundles, large pith and absence of secondary growth.
Identify and describe modifications of roots for storage, respiration, support and other special functions with named examples.
Given a described or observed modified root, identify its type and the function it serves, and relate the modification to the plant's habitat.
Analyse the functions of roots - anchorage, absorption, conduction and storage - and relate root structure and modifications to these functions.

chapter_summary.title: Root System - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Biology summary covers the root system of flowering plants: the types of root systems, the regions of a young root, the internal structure of dicot and monocot roots, the modifications of roots for special jobs, and the functions roots perform for the plant.

branches.label: Types
details: Tap root - from radicle, deep, dicots
Adventitious - from parts other than radicle

sections.heading: Types of root systems
bullets: The root develops from the radicle; it is underground, non-green and positively geotropic, and lacks leaves and buds.
Tap root system: the radicle forms a deep main root bearing laterals in acropetal order; typical of dicots (mustard, gram, mango).
Fibrous root system: the primary root dies and a cluster of thin equal roots arises from the stem base; typical of monocots (wheat, maize, grass).
Adventitious root system: roots arise from any part other than the radicle - stem, nodes or leaves (banyan prop roots, maize stilt roots).

sections.heading: Regions of a root
bullets: Root cap: a thimble-like cap of loose parenchyma that protects the growing tip and secretes lubricating mucilage.
Region of meristematic activity: small, thin-walled dividing cells just behind the cap that cause growth in length.
Region of elongation: cells stop dividing and enlarge rapidly, pushing the root deeper.
Region of maturation: cells mature and bear unicellular root hairs that absorb water and minerals.

sections.heading: Internal structure of a dicot root
bullets: From outside in: epidermis (epiblema) with root hairs, broad parenchymatous cortex, endodermis, pericycle, vascular bundles and pith.
The endodermis carries Casparian strips of suberin that force water to pass through the living cells - a check-post to the stele.
Vascular bundles are radial and exarch with only a few strands (di- to hexarch, usually tetrarch); pith is small or absent.
The pericycle gives rise to lateral roots and takes part in secondary growth in dicots.

sections.heading: Internal structure of a monocot root
bullets: A monocot root is broadly like a dicot root - epidermis, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle and radial exarch bundles.
It differs by having many (polyarch) vascular strands instead of a few.
It has a large, well-developed central pith.
It has no cambium and therefore shows no secondary growth.

sections.heading: Modifications and functions of roots
bullets: Storage roots swell with food: conical carrot, fusiform radish, napiform turnip, tuberous sweet potato.
Pneumatophores grow upward for respiration in marshy soil; prop and stilt roots give mechanical support.
Haustoria of parasites, nitrogen-fixing root nodules and velamen roots of orchids are other modifications.
Main functions: anchorage, absorption of water and minerals, conduction, storage, and soil binding.

key_takeaways: The root develops from the radicle, is positively geotropic and non-green, and all roots together form the root system.
Three root systems: tap (from radicle, deep, dicots), fibrous (thin equal roots from stem base, monocots) and adventitious (from parts other than the radicle).
A young root has four regions from the tip: root cap, meristematic region, elongation region and maturation region with root hairs.
A dicot root has radial exarch vascular bundles with few strands, an endodermis with Casparian strips, and little or no pith.
A monocot root differs by being polyarch, having a large pith and lacking secondary growth.
Roots are modified for storage (carrot, radish, sweet potato), respiration (pneumatophores) and support (prop, stilt roots).
The main functions of roots are anchorage, absorption of water and minerals, conduction, and storage of food.

glossary.definition: All the roots of a plant taken together; it may be a tap, fibrous or adventitious root system.
A root system in which the radicle forms a deep main root bearing lateral roots; typical of dicots.
A cluster of thin, thread-like roots of nearly equal size arising from the stem base; typical of monocots.
Roots that arise from any part of the plant other than the radicle, such as the stem, nodes or leaves.
A thimble-like cap of loose parenchyma that protects the growing root tip and secretes lubricating mucilage.
The zone of a root where cells mature into permanent tissues and bear absorbing root hairs.
A fine unicellular outgrowth of an epidermal cell that greatly increases surface area for absorbing water and minerals.
The outermost single layer of a root, without cuticle or stomata, whose cells extend as root hairs.
The innermost cortical layer of barrel-shaped cells bearing Casparian strips that regulate entry into the stele.
A band of waterproof suberin on the radial and transverse walls of endodermal cells that blocks the wall pathway of water.
The layer just inside the endodermis that gives rise to lateral roots and shares in secondary growth in dicots.
Xylem in which the oldest protoxylem lies towards the periphery and the metaxylem towards the centre, as in roots.
A vascular arrangement with many xylem and phloem strands, characteristic of the monocot root.
A negatively geotropic respiratory root of marshy plants that grows upward and bears pores for gas exchange.
A small swelling on the roots of legumes housing nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Root System (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly and to the point; draw and label diagrams only where asked. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Define a root system. Name the three types of root systems.
questions.answer: A root system is all the roots of a plant taken together, forming the underground descending part that develops (in the tap type) from the radicle. The three types are: (1) the tap root system, in which the radicle grows into a deep main root bearing laterals; (2) the fibrous root system, a cluster of thin roots of nearly equal size arising from the stem base; and (3) the adventitious root system, made of roots arising from parts of the plant other than the radicle.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the three named types.

questions.question: Distinguish between a tap root system and a fibrous root system, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: A tap root system develops from the radicle: it has one thick, deep main root (the tap root) that bears smaller lateral roots, and it is characteristic of dicots (example: mustard or gram). A fibrous root system has no persistent main root - the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by a cluster of thin, thread-like roots of nearly equal size that arise from the base of the stem; it is shallow and characteristic of monocots (example: wheat or grass).
questions.explanation: Contrast by origin, form, depth and plant group with examples.

questions.question: Name, in order from the tip, the four regions of a young root and state the main function of each.
questions.answer: From the tip upwards: (1) Root cap - protects the delicate growing tip and secretes lubricating mucilage; (2) Region of meristematic activity - actively dividing cells that bring about growth in length; (3) Region of elongation - cells enlarge and elongate, pushing the tip deeper; (4) Region of maturation - cells mature into permanent tissues and bear root hairs that absorb water and minerals.
questions.explanation: Four regions with the function of each.

questions.question: Describe the internal (transverse-section) structure of a dicot root from the outside inwards.
questions.answer: From outside inwards a dicot root shows: (1) Epidermis (epiblema) - a single outermost layer of thin-walled cells without cuticle or stomata, many extending as root hairs for absorption. (2) Cortex - several layers of thin-walled rounded parenchyma with intercellular spaces, which store food and pass water inward. (3) Endodermis - the innermost cortical layer of barrel-shaped cells whose radial and transverse walls bear Casparian strips of suberin that force water to move through the living cells, acting as a check-post. (4) Pericycle - a thin layer just inside the endodermis that gives rise to lateral roots and takes part in secondary growth. (5) Vascular bundles - xylem and phloem in separate radial strands; the xylem is exarch and there are only a few strands (di- to hexarch, usually tetrarch). (6) Pith - very small or almost absent because the xylem reaches nearly to the centre.
questions.explanation: Ordered account: epidermis, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, radial exarch bundles, little pith.

questions.question: State three ways in which the internal structure of a monocot root differs from that of a dicot root.
questions.answer: (1) The monocot root is polyarch - it has many (usually more than six) xylem and phloem strands, whereas the dicot root has only a few (di- to hexarch). (2) The monocot root has a large, well-developed central pith, whereas the dicot root has little or no pith. (3) The monocot root lacks a cambium and shows no secondary growth, whereas the dicot root undergoes secondary growth.
questions.explanation: Three differences: polyarch, large pith, no secondary growth.

questions.question: What are storage roots? Name the storage-root type found in carrot, radish and turnip.
questions.answer: Storage roots are roots that become swollen and fleshy by storing large amounts of reserve food such as starch and sugars. In these three the tap root itself stores food: carrot has a conical root (broad at the top, tapering downward), radish has a fusiform root (spindle-shaped, swollen in the middle and tapering at both ends), and turnip has a napiform root (top-shaped, swollen and rounded, tapering sharply below).
questions.explanation: Definition plus conical, fusiform and napiform shapes.

questions.question: A mangrove tree in a waterlogged swamp has some roots growing vertically upwards out of the mud. Name these roots and explain their function.
questions.answer: These upward-growing roots are pneumatophores (respiratory roots). Mangroves grow in marshy, saline, waterlogged soil that is poor in oxygen, so some roots grow vertically upward (negatively geotropic) into the air. They bear small pores (pneumathodes or lenticels) through which air enters and reaches the underground roots, allowing them to respire in the oxygen-poor mud.
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores; upward growth and pores supply oxygen to roots in waterlogged soil.

questions.question: Explain the main functions of roots and show how root structure and modifications help carry out these functions.
questions.answer: Anchorage: roots fix the plant firmly in the soil and hold the shoot upright; deep tap roots and spreading fibrous roots both give a firm grip, and stilt and prop roots add extra support. Absorption: root hairs in the region of maturation enormously increase surface area and absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil; the epidermis and cortex pass this inward. Conduction: the radial xylem carries absorbed water and minerals up to the stem and leaves, while food can move down to be stored. Storage: fleshy modified roots such as carrot, radish and sweet potato store starch and sugars for later use. Special functions come from modifications - pneumatophores allow respiration in marshy soil, root nodules with Rhizobium fix atmospheric nitrogen, and roots also bind the soil and check erosion. Thus each structural feature (root hairs, xylem, fleshy tissue, upward or supporting roots) is matched to a function.
questions.explanation: Anchorage, absorption, conduction, storage plus special functions, each linked to structure or a modification.

questions.question: What are adventitious roots? Give two examples of adventitious roots that provide mechanical support.
questions.answer: Adventitious roots are roots that arise from any part of the plant other than the radicle - from the stem, nodes, branches or leaves. Two supporting examples are: prop roots of the banyan tree, which hang down from horizontal branches, reach the soil and thicken into pillar-like supports; and stilt roots of maize and sugarcane, which grow obliquely from the lower nodes of the stem into the soil to brace the plant.
questions.explanation: Definition plus prop roots and stilt roots as supporting examples.

questions.question: What is the Casparian strip and why is it important?
questions.answer: The Casparian strip is a band of waterproof, corky material (suberin) deposited on the radial and transverse walls of the endodermal cells in the root. It is important because it blocks the movement of water and dissolved minerals through the cell walls of the endodermis and forces them to pass instead through the living cytoplasm of the endodermal cells. In this way the endodermis acts as a check-post that controls exactly what enters the central vascular cylinder (stele).
questions.explanation: Suberin band on endodermal walls; forces water through living cells, controlling entry to the stele.

questions.question: The root develops from which part of the germinating seed?
questions.explanation: The radicle of the embryo grows into the primary root.

questions.question: Fixing the plant firmly in the soil is the function called ______.
questions.explanation: Anchorage holds the plant upright.

questions.question: Define a root and give two features that distinguish it from a stem.
questions.answer: A root is the underground, non-green, descending part of the plant that develops from the radicle and lacks leaves and buds. Two distinguishing features: (1) it grows towards gravity (positively geotropic) and away from light, whereas the stem grows upward; and (2) it bears no nodes, internodes, leaves or buds, and its epidermis bears root hairs instead of stomata.
questions.explanation: Definition plus geotropism and absence of leaves/buds.

questions.question: Give one example each of a plant with a tap root, a fibrous root and an adventitious supporting root.
questions.answer: Tap root: mustard (or gram, mango). Fibrous root: wheat (or grass, maize). Adventitious supporting root: prop roots of banyan (or stilt roots of maize/sugarcane).
questions.explanation: One example for each of the three types.

questions.question: Why are the fibrous roots of a grass described as adventitious?
questions.answer: In a grass the primary root that came from the radicle is short-lived and soon dies. The cluster of thin roots that replaces it does not develop from the radicle but grows out from the base of the stem. Since adventitious roots are, by definition, roots that arise from any part of the plant other than the radicle, these stem-borne fibrous roots are adventitious in origin.
questions.explanation: They arise from the stem base, not the radicle, hence adventitious.

questions.question: List three differences between a tap root system and a fibrous root system.
questions.answer: (1) Origin: a tap root develops from the radicle, while a fibrous root system arises from the stem base after the primary root dies. (2) Form: a tap root system has one thick main root with laterals, while a fibrous system is a cluster of thin roots of nearly equal size. (3) Depth and group: a tap root goes deep and is typical of dicots, while fibrous roots are shallow and typical of monocots.
questions.explanation: Origin, form, depth/plant group.

questions.question: Describe the structure and function of the root cap.
questions.answer: The root cap is a thimble-like cap of loosely arranged parenchyma cells covering the very tip of the root. Its function is to protect the delicate growing tip as the root is pushed through hard, abrasive soil. Its outer cells are continually worn away and replaced from within, and the cap secretes a slimy mucilage that lubricates the passage of the root through the soil.
questions.explanation: Loose parenchyma cap; protects tip and secretes lubricating mucilage.

questions.question: Why are root hairs important for a plant? Where are they found?
questions.answer: Root hairs are found in the region of maturation of a young root, each being a fine, tubular, unicellular outgrowth of an epidermal cell. They are important because they enormously increase the surface area of the root and are the chief site for the absorption of water and dissolved mineral salts from the soil. Without them the plant could not take up enough water and nutrients.
questions.explanation: Maturation region; increase surface area for absorption.

questions.question: What happens in the region of elongation of a root?
questions.answer: In the region of elongation the cells produced by the meristematic region stop dividing and instead enlarge and elongate rapidly, taking in water and greatly increasing their length. This elongation pushes the root tip deeper into the soil, and the cells also begin to differentiate.
questions.explanation: Cells enlarge/elongate, pushing the tip deeper.

questions.question: What is the endodermis? State its special feature and role.
questions.answer: The endodermis is the innermost single layer of the cortex, made of compact barrel-shaped cells. Its special feature is the Casparian strip - a band of waterproof suberin on the radial and transverse walls. Its role is to act as a check-post: the Casparian strips block water from moving through the cell walls and force all incoming water and minerals to pass through the living cytoplasm of the endodermal cells, so the endodermis controls what enters the vascular cylinder.
questions.explanation: Innermost cortex layer with Casparian strips; regulates entry to the stele.

questions.question: Describe the vascular tissue arrangement in a dicot root.
questions.answer: In a dicot root the xylem and phloem occur as separate strands lying on different radii - a radial arrangement. The xylem is exarch, meaning the first-formed protoxylem lies towards the outside (periphery) and the metaxylem towards the centre. There are only a few strands, usually two to six (di- to hexarch), most commonly tetrarch, and the central pith is small or almost absent.
questions.explanation: Radial, exarch, few strands (usually tetrarch), little pith.

questions.question: What is the pericycle and what does it produce in a dicot root?
questions.answer: The pericycle is a layer, one or a few cells thick, of thin-walled cells lying just inside the endodermis. In a dicot root it gives rise to lateral (branch) roots and also takes part in secondary growth by producing part of the vascular cambium and the cork cambium.
questions.explanation: Layer inside endodermis; forms lateral roots and shares in secondary growth.

questions.question: How does a monocot root differ from a dicot root in its vascular tissue and pith?
questions.answer: In its vascular tissue a monocot root is polyarch - it has many (usually more than six) xylem and phloem strands arranged in a ring - whereas a dicot root has only a few strands (di- to hexarch). In its pith a monocot root has a large, well-developed central pith, whereas a dicot root has a small pith or almost none. In both, however, the bundles are radial and the xylem is exarch.
questions.explanation: Monocot: polyarch and large pith; dicot: few strands and little pith.

questions.question: Why does a monocot root not increase in thickness during its life?
questions.answer: A monocot root does not increase in thickness because it lacks a vascular cambium. Without a cambium there is no secondary growth, so no new xylem and phloem are added and the root keeps the same diameter throughout its life.
questions.explanation: No cambium, hence no secondary growth or thickening.

questions.question: List the features that are common to both dicot and monocot roots.
questions.answer: Both dicot and monocot roots have: an epidermis (epiblema) that may bear root hairs and lacks a cuticle; a broad parenchymatous cortex with intercellular spaces; an endodermis whose cells carry Casparian strips; a pericycle just inside the endodermis; vascular bundles arranged radially with the xylem exarch (protoxylem outward). They differ only in the number of vascular strands, the size of the pith and the presence of secondary growth.
questions.explanation: Epidermis, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, radial exarch bundles.

questions.question: Name the storage-root shapes of carrot, radish and turnip.
questions.answer: Carrot has a conical storage root (broad at the top and tapering downward). Radish has a fusiform storage root (spindle-shaped, swollen in the middle and tapering at both ends). Turnip has a napiform storage root (top-shaped, swollen and rounded above, tapering sharply below).
questions.explanation: Conical, fusiform and napiform respectively.

questions.question: What are pneumatophores? Why are they needed by mangrove plants?
questions.answer: Pneumatophores are special respiratory roots that grow vertically upward (negatively geotropic) out of the mud into the air. They are needed by mangrove plants because these plants grow in marshy, saline, waterlogged soil where oxygen is very scarce around the underground roots. The pneumatophores bear small pores (pneumathodes or lenticels) through which air enters and reaches the buried roots, allowing them to respire.
questions.explanation: Upward respiratory roots with pores; supply oxygen to roots in waterlogged soil.

questions.question: Distinguish between prop roots and stilt roots with one example of each.
questions.answer: Prop roots grow downward from the horizontal branches of a tree, reach the soil and thicken into pillar-like supports for the spreading crown - example: the banyan tree. Stilt roots grow obliquely downward from the lower nodes of the stem into the soil to brace the plant - examples: maize and sugarcane. Both are adventitious supporting roots, but prop roots come from branches while stilt roots come from stem nodes.
questions.explanation: Prop roots from branches (banyan); stilt roots from lower nodes (maize).

questions.question: What are root nodules and what is their importance?
questions.answer: Root nodules are small swellings on the roots of leguminous plants (such as gram, pea and bean) that house symbiotic nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria. Their importance is that the bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen compounds that the plant can use, and they also enrich the soil with nitrogen, which benefits later crops.
questions.explanation: Swellings with Rhizobium that fix atmospheric nitrogen and enrich soil.

questions.question: A gardener notices that a money plant climbs a wall using small roots at its nodes. Name and explain this modification.
questions.answer: These are climbing (clinging) roots, a kind of adventitious root that arises from the nodes of weak-stemmed climbers such as the money plant (Pothos) and betel. They grow out at the nodes and cling to the support (a wall, tree or pole), helping the weak stem to climb and stay attached as it grows upward.
questions.explanation: Adventitious climbing roots from nodes that cling to a support.

questions.question: In a kitchen you have a carrot, a radish and a sweet potato. Classify each by the kind of root that is eaten.
questions.answer: The carrot and the radish are modified TAP roots that store food: the carrot is a conical tap root and the radish is a fusiform tap root. The sweet potato is different - it is a tuberous ADVENTITIOUS root, that is, a swollen food-storing root that arises from the stem, not from the tap root. So two of them (carrot, radish) are storage tap roots and one (sweet potato) is a storage adventitious root.
questions.explanation: Carrot and radish are storage tap roots; sweet potato is a tuberous adventitious root.

questions.question: State any three functions of roots.
questions.answer: (1) Anchorage - roots fix the plant firmly in the soil and hold the shoot upright. (2) Absorption - roots, chiefly through their root hairs, absorb water and dissolved mineral salts from the soil. (3) Conduction - the absorbed water and minerals are conducted through the xylem to the stem and leaves (and food may move down to be stored). Storage of reserve food is a further important function.
questions.explanation: Anchorage, absorption, conduction (and storage).

questions.question: A vegetable is spindle-shaped, thickest in the middle and tapering at both ends. Name its shape and the crop.
questions.answer: This shape is called fusiform (spindle-shaped). The crop with such a modified fleshy tap root is the radish. The root is swollen in the middle and tapers towards both the top and the bottom, storing reserve food.
questions.explanation: Fusiform shape identifies the radish tap root.

questions.question: How is the structure of the root well suited to absorption of water?
questions.answer: The root is well suited to absorption in several ways. In the region of maturation the epidermal cells extend into countless fine root hairs, which greatly increase the surface area in contact with soil water. The thin-walled epidermis lacks a cuticle, so water passes in easily. Behind it the parenchymatous cortex with air spaces lets water move inward, and the endodermis with its Casparian strips channels the water into the xylem, which then conducts it upward. Together these features make the root an efficient absorbing and conducting organ.
questions.explanation: Root hairs increase area; thin epidermis, cortex and xylem move water inward and up.

questions.question: Describe the three types of root systems with their origin, form and examples.
questions.answer: TAP ROOT SYSTEM: it develops from the radicle, which grows into a thick, deep main root called the tap root. From this main root arise smaller lateral (secondary and tertiary) roots in acropetal order. The tap root grows vertically downward, anchors the plant firmly and can draw water from deep soil. It is the normal root system of most dicots - for example mustard, gram, mango and neem. FIBROUS ROOT SYSTEM: here the primary root from the radicle is short-lived and soon dies. It is replaced by a cluster of thin, thread-like roots of nearly equal size that grow from the base of the stem. These shallow roots spread out and bind the top soil well. It is typical of most monocots - for example wheat, maize, rice and grasses. ADVENTITIOUS ROOT SYSTEM: this consists of roots that arise from any part of the plant OTHER than the radicle - from the stem, nodes, branches or leaves. Examples are the prop roots of banyan, the stilt roots of maize and sugarcane, and roots from a stem cutting of rose or sugarcane. Adventitious roots may do normal work or special jobs such as support or storage.
questions.explanation: Tap (radicle, deep, dicots), fibrous (stem base, monocots) and adventitious (other parts) with examples.

questions.question: With reference to a young root, describe its four regions from the tip upwards.
questions.answer: ROOT CAP: the very tip is covered by a thimble-like cap of loosely arranged parenchyma. It protects the delicate growing tip as the root is forced through hard soil; its worn outer cells are replaced from within and it secretes a lubricating mucilage. REGION OF MERISTEMATIC ACTIVITY: just behind the cap is a short zone of small, thin-walled, densely cytoplasmic cells with prominent nuclei that divide repeatedly by mitosis, bringing about growth in length; it bears no root hairs. REGION OF ELONGATION: above this the newly formed cells stop dividing and enlarge and elongate rapidly, taking in water and increasing greatly in length, which pushes the tip deeper; the cells also begin to differentiate. REGION OF MATURATION (root-hair region): still higher the cells reach full size and mature into permanent tissues, and the epidermal cells grow out into numerous fine, unicellular root hairs. These root hairs greatly increase surface area and are the chief site of absorption of water and minerals; the older part above may bear lateral roots.
questions.explanation: Root cap, meristematic, elongation and maturation regions, each described with its role.

questions.question: Draw and describe (in words) the internal structure of a dicot root as seen in transverse section.
questions.answer: In transverse section a young dicot root shows, from outside inward: EPIDERMIS (EPIBLEMA) - a single outermost layer of thin-walled cells without cuticle or stomata, many extending as unicellular root hairs; it protects and absorbs. CORTEX - several layers of thin-walled, rounded parenchyma with conspicuous intercellular spaces, storing food and passing water inward. ENDODERMIS - the innermost cortical layer of compact barrel-shaped cells whose radial and transverse walls bear Casparian strips of suberin; these force incoming water to pass through the living cells, so the endodermis controls entry into the stele. PERICYCLE - a thin layer just inside the endodermis that gives rise to lateral roots and shares in secondary growth. VASCULAR BUNDLES - the xylem and phloem lie as separate strands on different radii (radial); the xylem is exarch, and there are only a few strands (di- to hexarch, usually tetrarch). PITH - very small or almost absent because the xylem reaches nearly to the centre. Between the xylem and phloem lie thin-walled conjunctive parenchyma cells.
questions.explanation: Ordered word-description: epidermis, cortex, endodermis + Casparian strips, pericycle, radial exarch bundles, small pith.

questions.question: Compare the internal structure of a dicot root and a monocot root, listing their similarities and differences.
questions.answer: SIMILARITIES: both roots show, from outside inward, an epidermis (epiblema) that may bear root hairs and lacks a cuticle; a broad parenchymatous cortex with intercellular spaces; an endodermis of barrel-shaped cells bearing Casparian strips that regulate water entry; a pericycle just inside the endodermis that produces lateral roots; and vascular bundles that are arranged radially with the xylem exarch (protoxylem towards the outside). DIFFERENCES: (1) Number of vascular strands - a dicot root has only a few (di- to hexarch, usually tetrarch), whereas a monocot root is polyarch with many strands. (2) Pith - a dicot root has a small pith or almost none, whereas a monocot root has a large, well-developed central pith. (3) Secondary growth - a dicot root has a cambium and undergoes secondary growth (so the pericycle also forms vascular and cork cambium), whereas a monocot root lacks a cambium and shows no secondary growth (its pericycle forms only lateral roots). These anatomical differences are commonly used to identify the two under a microscope.
questions.explanation: Shared layers (epidermis to radial exarch bundles) vs differences in strand number, pith and secondary growth.

questions.question: Describe the various modifications of roots for storage and support with examples.
questions.answer: STORAGE MODIFICATIONS: roots may swell with reserve food (starch and sugars). In the tap-root storage type the main root becomes fleshy - conical in carrot, fusiform (spindle-shaped) in radish, and napiform (top-shaped) in turnip and beet. In some plants adventitious roots store food, as in the tuberous roots of sweet potato and the fascicled (clustered) roots of dahlia and Asparagus. SUPPORT MODIFICATIONS: several adventitious roots give mechanical support. Prop (pillar) roots hang from the horizontal branches of the banyan, reach the soil and thicken into pillars that hold up the huge crown. Stilt roots grow obliquely from the lower nodes of the stem into the soil to brace the plant, as in maize, sugarcane and screw-pine. Climbing roots arise at the nodes of weak-stemmed climbers such as money plant and betel and cling to a support. Thus by becoming fleshy, pillar-like, oblique or clinging, roots are modified to store food or to give the plant extra support.
questions.explanation: Storage: conical/fusiform/napiform tap roots and tuberous/fascicled adventitious roots; support: prop, stilt and climbing roots.

questions.question: For each situation, name the root modification and explain how it helps the plant: (a) a mangrove in a tidal swamp, (b) a banyan tree with a very wide crown, (c) a leafless dodder twining on a host, (d) a gram plant enriching the soil.
questions.answer: (a) Mangrove in a tidal swamp: it forms pneumatophores - respiratory roots that grow vertically up out of the oxygen-poor, waterlogged mud and bear pores through which air reaches the buried roots, letting them respire. (b) Banyan with a wide crown: it forms prop (pillar) roots that hang from the branches, reach the ground and thicken into pillars, giving mechanical support so the very wide, heavy crown does not collapse. (c) Leafless dodder (Cuscuta) on a host: it forms haustoria - sucking roots that penetrate the host stem and absorb food and water from it, since the parasite cannot make its own food. (d) Gram plant enriching the soil: it forms root nodules housing Rhizobium bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen into usable compounds, feeding the plant and enriching the soil with nitrogen. Each modification is matched to the plant's need in its particular habitat.
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores (respiration), prop roots (support), haustoria (parasitic absorption), root nodules (nitrogen fixation).

questions.question: Explain the main functions of the root and relate each to a structural feature of the root.
questions.answer: ANCHORAGE: the root fixes the plant firmly in the soil and holds the shoot upright; this is served by the deep, strong tap root or the widely spreading fibrous roots, and by supporting stilt and prop roots. ABSORPTION: the root takes up water and dissolved minerals; this is served by the countless fine root hairs in the region of maturation and by the thin, cuticle-free epidermis, which together give a huge absorbing surface. CONDUCTION: water and minerals must reach the rest of the plant; this is served by the radial exarch xylem, which conducts them upward, while phloem can bring food down. STORAGE: reserve food is kept for later use; this is served by the parenchymatous cortex and, in modified roots such as carrot, radish and sweet potato, by fleshy food-filled tissue. Additional functions - soil binding by spreading roots, respiration by pneumatophores, and nitrogen fixation by nodulated roots - are likewise matched to particular structures. Thus every major function of the root can be traced to a specific structural feature.
questions.explanation: Anchorage-tap/fibrous roots; absorption-root hairs; conduction-xylem; storage-cortex/fleshy roots.

questions.question: What is meant by a root and a root system? Explain the difference between a tap root and adventitious roots.
questions.answer: A ROOT is the underground, non-green, descending part of a flowering plant that normally develops from the radicle of the seed; it lacks leaves, buds and nodes, grows towards gravity and absorbs water and minerals. A ROOT SYSTEM is all the roots of a plant taken together, and it may be of the tap, fibrous or adventitious type. A TAP ROOT is the single thick main root that develops directly from the radicle and grows deep into the soil, bearing smaller lateral roots along its length (as in mustard or mango). ADVENTITIOUS ROOTS, in contrast, do not develop from the radicle at all; they arise from other parts of the plant - the stem, nodes, branches or leaves - as in the prop roots of banyan, the stilt roots of maize or the roots of a stem cutting. So the key difference is one of origin: a tap root comes from the radicle, whereas adventitious roots come from parts other than the radicle.
questions.explanation: Root and root-system defined; tap root from radicle vs adventitious roots from other parts.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student pulls out two young seedlings from a nursery. In seedling A there is one thick main root going straight down with several thin side roots. In seedling B there is a bunch of thin roots of almost equal size spreading from the base of the shoot, with no single main root.
(a) Name the root system of A and of B.
(b) From which part of the seed did the main root of A develop?
(c) To which group (dicot/monocot) does each seedling most likely belong?
(d) Which seedling would bind the surface soil better and why?
questions.answer: (a) A has a tap root system; B has a fibrous root system. (b) The main root of A developed from the radicle of the embryo. (c) A (tap root) is most likely a dicot; B (fibrous root) is most likely a monocot. (d) B, the fibrous-rooted seedling, would bind the surface soil better because its many thin roots spread out just below the surface and hold the top soil together, which is why grasses are used to check soil erosion.
questions.explanation: Tap vs fibrous identification, radicle origin, dicot/monocot, and soil-binding by fibrous roots.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Under a microscope a young root tip shows, from the very tip upwards, first a protective cap, then a zone of tiny dividing cells, then a zone where cells are getting longer, and finally a zone covered with fine hair-like structures.
(a) Name the four regions in order.
(b) Which region protects the tip and how?
(c) What are the hair-like structures and what do they do?
(d) In which region does the root actually grow in length?
questions.answer: (a) In order from the tip: root cap, region of meristematic activity, region of elongation, and region of maturation. (b) The root cap protects the tip; it is a cap of loose parenchyma that covers the delicate growing point and secretes a lubricating mucilage as the root pushes through the soil. (c) The hair-like structures are root hairs, unicellular outgrowths of epidermal cells; they greatly increase surface area and absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil. (d) The root grows in length mainly in the region of meristematic activity (by cell division) together with the region of elongation (by cell enlargement).
questions.explanation: Four regions, protective cap, absorbing root hairs, and growth zones.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a transverse section of a young root, a special innermost layer of the cortex has cells whose side walls carry a waterproof corky band. Because of this band, water cannot slip through the walls of these cells.
(a) Name this innermost cortical layer.
(b) What is the waterproof band called and what is it made of?
(c) Through what path must water now enter the vascular cylinder?
(d) What is the value of this arrangement to the plant?
questions.answer: (a) The innermost cortical layer is the endodermis. (b) The waterproof band is the Casparian strip, made of suberin (a corky material). (c) Because the walls are blocked, water and minerals must now pass through the living cytoplasm of the endodermal cells to reach the vascular cylinder. (d) The value is that the endodermis acts as a check-post: it controls exactly what enters the stele, preventing the free, unregulated leakage of water and solutes and letting the plant regulate uptake into the xylem.
questions.explanation: Endodermis, Casparian strip of suberin, symplast path, and regulation of entry to the stele.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two root sections are compared. Section X has only four xylem strands and almost no pith, and it shows a cambium. Section Y has many xylem strands, a large central pith, and no cambium.
(a) Which section is a dicot root and which is a monocot root?
(b) What term describes the many-stranded condition of Y?
(c) Which section can undergo secondary growth and why?
(d) State one feature common to both X and Y.
questions.answer: (a) Section X is a dicot root (few strands, little pith, cambium present) and Section Y is a monocot root (many strands, large pith, no cambium). (b) The many-stranded condition of Y is described as polyarch. (c) Section X (the dicot root) can undergo secondary growth because it has a cambium, whereas Y lacks a cambium and cannot. (d) A feature common to both is the endodermis bearing Casparian strips (also acceptable: radial arrangement of bundles, exarch xylem, or a pericycle).
questions.explanation: Dicot vs monocot from strand number/pith/cambium, polyarch term, secondary growth, shared endodermis.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a market you see carrot, radish, turnip and sweet potato, all sold as underground vegetables. On cutting them open they are seen to be full of stored food.
(a) Which of these are modified TAP roots?
(b) Name the shape of the carrot root and of the radish root.
(c) Which one is a modified ADVENTITIOUS root?
(d) What is the general name for such food-filled roots?
questions.answer: (a) Carrot, radish and turnip are modified tap roots. (b) The carrot root is conical and the radish root is fusiform (spindle-shaped). (c) The sweet potato is a modified adventitious root (a tuberous root). (d) The general name for such swollen, food-filled roots is storage roots (fleshy roots).
questions.explanation: Tap vs adventitious storage roots; conical and fusiform shapes; storage roots as the general term.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In a coastal mangrove swamp, the soil is waterlogged and salty and contains very little air. Some trees there send up pencil-like roots from the mud into the air, and these roots have tiny pores.
(a) Name these special roots.
(b) Why are they needed in this habitat?
(c) What is the function of the tiny pores on them?
(d) In which direction do they grow with respect to gravity?
questions.answer: (a) These special roots are pneumatophores (respiratory roots). (b) They are needed because the waterlogged, saline mud has very little oxygen, so the underground roots cannot get enough air for respiration. (c) The tiny pores (pneumathodes or lenticels) allow air to enter and pass down to the buried roots so that they can respire. (d) They grow vertically upward, that is, away from gravity - they are negatively geotropic.
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores supply oxygen to roots in oxygen-poor waterlogged soil; grow upward via pores.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A very old banyan tree has a huge spreading crown supported by many thick, pillar-like roots that hang down from its branches to the ground. Nearby, maize plants stand firm with slanting roots coming out of the lower part of their stems.
(a) Name the banyan's supporting roots and the maize's supporting roots.
(b) From which part of the plant does each arise?
(c) What common function do both serve?
(d) To which category of roots (by origin) do both belong?
questions.answer: (a) The banyan's supporting roots are prop (pillar) roots and the maize's are stilt roots. (b) The prop roots arise from the horizontal branches of the banyan, while the stilt roots arise from the lower nodes of the maize stem. (c) Both serve the common function of giving mechanical support, holding up the heavy crown of the banyan and bracing the maize plant. (d) Both belong to the adventitious roots, because they arise from parts other than the radicle.
questions.explanation: Prop vs stilt roots, their origins, shared support function, and adventitious category.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A farmer rotates his crops. In one season he grows a legume such as gram, whose roots bear small swellings. He notices that the field is more fertile for the next cereal crop, so he does not need to add as much nitrogen fertiliser.
(a) Name the small swellings on the legume roots.
(b) What organism lives inside them?
(c) How do they make the field more fertile?
(d) Name this useful process.
questions.answer: (a) The small swellings are root nodules. (b) Nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria live inside them (in a symbiotic association with the legume). (c) They make the field more fertile because the bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into nitrogen compounds that plants can use, leaving the soil enriched with nitrogen for the next crop. (d) This useful process is (biological) nitrogen fixation.
questions.explanation: Root nodules with Rhizobium carry out nitrogen fixation, enriching the soil.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A young plant is uprooted, its root hairs are damaged and many are lost. Over the next days the plant wilts even though the soil is moist.
(a) Which main function of the root has been affected?
(b) Why does damage to root hairs cause wilting?
(c) Name the tissue that would have carried the absorbed water upward.
(d) Besides absorption, state two other functions of roots.
questions.answer: (a) The function of absorption of water (and minerals) has been affected. (b) Root hairs provide most of the surface area for absorbing water; when they are lost the plant cannot take up enough water from the soil, so more water is lost by the leaves than is absorbed and the plant wilts. (c) The xylem would have carried the absorbed water upward to the shoot. (d) Two other functions of roots are anchorage (fixing the plant in the soil) and storage of reserve food (also acceptable: conduction, soil binding).
questions.explanation: Absorption via root hairs; loss causes wilting; xylem conducts water; other functions anchorage/storage.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

On a bare hill slope the soil is being washed away by rain. An expert advises planting grasses and certain trees to hold the soil, and points out that some of these plants also store food underground and take up deep water.
(a) Which property of grass roots helps to hold the slope soil?
(b) Which root system is present in grasses?
(c) Name a root function that lets some plants store food underground.
(d) Which type of root reaches deep water and gives firm anchorage?
questions.answer: (a) The dense, spreading, shallow nature of grass roots helps to bind and hold the surface soil, checking erosion. (b) Grasses have a fibrous root system. (c) The storage function of roots lets plants keep reserve food underground (in fleshy storage roots). (d) A deep tap root reaches deep water and gives firm anchorage to the plant.
questions.explanation: Fibrous roots bind soil; storage function; deep tap root for deep water and anchorage.
